titre: The Raft of the Medusa Was Called “Scène de naufrage” (Shipwreck Scene) at the 1819 Salon
accroche: In the 1819 Salon catalog, Géricault's painting is No. 510 and carries a title with no ship's name, even though a survivors' account was already in circulation.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the catalog of the Salon that opens on August 25, 1819, at the Royal Museum, the entry for Théodore Géricault runs a single line: number 510 and the title “Scène de naufrage” (Shipwreck Scene). No ship's name, no date, no place. The canvas that the Louvre now calls *Le Radeau de la Méduse* (The Raft of the Medusa) enters the exhibition under a title that could describe any shipwreck.

## What the Catalog Doesn't Say

The shipwreck itself is known in detail. The frigate *La Méduse* leaves the Île d'Aix on June 17, 1816, with the Senegal expedition and runs aground on July 2, at 3:15 in the afternoon, on a bank off the African coast. According to the authors' account, the commander, Chaumareys, leaves the frigate in his boat; 150 people are entrusted to a makeshift raft.

Two of them, the naval surgeon Jean-Baptiste Henri Savigny and the engineer-geographer Alexandre Corréard, publish in Paris their *Naufrage de la frégate la Méduse* (Shipwreck of the Frigate Medusa), signed “both shipwrecked from the raft.” The second edition, from 1818, sums up the toll in one sentence: “Of the 150 abandoned, only 15 were saved.” Five of them still die at Saint-Louis. Thirteen days of drifting separate the abandonment from the rescue.

The Louvre repeats these figures: 150 people, 13 days, 15 survivors. It also notes that Géricault, to prepare his painting, met with survivors.

## A Title That Comes From Outside

The catalog therefore repeats nothing of what the public could read elsewhere. The name of the frigate, the figures from the raft, the fate of the survivors: all of that was in an already published book, whose second edition dates from 1818, not on the Salon page. The “Radeau de la Méduse” label we use today is not the one in the catalog.

This shifts a question often put to the canvas, that of intention. The catalog does not allow us to claim that Géricault wanted to hide the name; it establishes only that the name does not appear there. To know what the canvas is about, one has to look elsewhere for what the Salon page does not give.

When did the label change, and under whose pen? The catalog does not say, and that is where one would have to look.

carte.punch: At the 1819 Salon, the Raft of the Medusa was called “Scène de naufrage” (Shipwreck Scene).
carte.idee: The 1819 Salon catalog lists Géricault's canvas as No. 510 under a title with no ship's name. The figures of the tragedy, 150 on the raft and 15 saved, were in the account by Savigny and Corréard, published before the Salon.

quiz.question: According to the account by Savigny and Corréard (1818), how many of the people left on the raft were saved?
quiz.explication: The account states: “Of the 150 abandoned, only 15 were saved,” and five more die at Saint-Louis. The other figures, 60, 100, or 13 survivors, do not appear in the text, and 13 is the number of days adrift.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the 1819 Salon catalog, under what title is Géricault's painting listed?
choix: Le Radeau de la Méduse (The Raft of the Medusa)
Naufrage de la frégate la Méduse (Shipwreck of the Frigate Medusa)
Scène de naufrage de la Méduse (Shipwreck Scene of the Medusa)
Scène de naufrage (Shipwreck Scene), with no ship's name
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1819 Salon catalog lists the canvas as number 510 under the title Scène de naufrage (Shipwreck Scene), without mentioning the name of the frigate La Méduse.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the account by Savigny and Corréard, what does Commander Chaumareys do at the time of the shipwreck?
choix: He stays aboard the frigate until the final rescue
He leaves the frigate in his boat, leaving 150 people on a raft
He himself organizes the building of the raft before settling onto it
He dies in the shipwreck before the raft is abandoned
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the survivors' account, Commander Chaumareys leaves the frigate in his boat while 150 people are entrusted to a makeshift raft.
